function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL and retrieves data as specified by the parameters. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to which the GET request is sent. It is expected to be a well-formed HTTP or HTTPS URL.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: A dictionary of HTTP headers to send with the request. Each key-value pair represents a header name and its value.

timeout.description: The number of seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, as a float, or a (connect_timeout, read_timeout) tuple. This is a float type value.

lat.description: Latitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

lon.description: Longitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters to append to the URL for the GET request.

allow_redirects.description: Determines if HTTP redirections (301, 302, etc.) should be followed.

auth.description: A tuple representing the user credentials for HTTP authentication, typically in the form of (username, password).

cert.description: Path to an SSL certificate file to verify the peer, or a tuple of (certificate file, key file).

cookies.description: A dictionary of cookies to send with the request. The key is the cookie name and the value is the cookie value.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: A dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy.

stream.description: If True, the response content will not be downloaded immediately but streamed.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not, or a path to a CA bundle if verification is needed.

message.content:
When you’re tracking currency valuations (e.g., exchange rates, spot prices, or historical rates) over time, you want a structure that: 1. **Keeps data sorted by time** – so you can quickly find the rate for a given timestamp or interpolate between two points. 2. **Supports fast inserts** – new daily/weekly/monthly rates are added regularly. 3. **Allows efficient range queries** – e.g., “give me all rates between Jan 1 and Jan 31”. 4. **Handles sparse data** – you might have gaps (weekends, holidays) without rates. With those requirements in mind, the most common and effective data structures are: | Data Structure | Why it’s good for currency valuations | Typical use‑case | |----------------|---------------------------------------|------------------| | **Sorted list / array of tuples** (`[(timestamp, rate), …]`) | • Simple, memory‑efficient.
• Binary search gives O(log n) lookup for a specific time.
• Append at the end is O(1) amortized. | Small to medium datasets (e.g., a few years of daily rates). | | **Balanced binary search tree** (e.g., `std::map` in C++, `TreeMap` in Java, `sortedcontainers.SortedDict` in Python) | • Keeps keys (timestamps) sorted automatically.
• O(log n) insert, delete, and lookup.
• Supports range queries via iterators. | When you need frequent inserts/deletes and range queries, especially if the dataset grows large. | | **Time‑series database (TSDB)** (e.g., InfluxDB, TimescaleDB, Prometheus) | • Optimized for high‑volume, continuous data.
• Built‑in compression, down‑sampling, and retention policies.
• Powerful query language for aggregates, interpolation, and window functions. | Production systems that ingest thousands of rates per second, need long‑term storage, and require complex analytics. | | **Key‑value store with time‑based keys** (e.g., Redis sorted sets, DynamoDB with composite keys) | • Fast read/write with in‑memory caching.
• Sorted sets allow range queries by score (timestamp). | Real‑time dashboards or services that need sub‑millisecond latency. | | **Immutable persistent data structure** (e.g., functional persistent trees) | • Enables versioning of the entire series (useful for audit trails).
• Each update returns a new root, sharing unchanged nodes. | Systems that need to keep a full history of every change for compliance. | ### Recommendation for most scenarios For **most applications**—especially when you’re building a service that stores daily or hourly rates for a handful of currencies—the **sorted list (array) of `(timestamp, rate)` tuples** is usually the simplest and fastest: ```python # Python example rates = [] # list of (timestamp, rate) # Insert new rate (append, then keep sorted if needed) rates.append((datetime.utcnow(), 1.2345)) rates.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # keep sorted; or use bisect.insort # Lookup rate for a specific time (binary search) import bisect def get_rate_at(ts): idx = bisect.bisect_left(rates, (ts, -float('inf'))) if idx < len(rates) and rates[idx][0] == ts: return rates[idx][1] # interpolate or return None ``` If you expect **high write throughput** or need **range queries** (e.g., “average rate over the last month”), switch to a **balanced BST** or a **TSDB**. For real‑time dashboards, a **Redis sorted set** can give you sub‑millisecond lookups. ### Quick checklist | Need | Suggested structure | Notes | |------|---------------------|-------| | Simple, small dataset | Sorted list | O(log n) lookup, O(1) append | | Frequent inserts/deletes | Balanced BST | O(log n) ops | | Long‑term storage, high volume | TSDB | Compression, retention | | Real‑time analytics | Redis sorted set | In‑memory, fast | | Full audit trail | Persistent tree | Immutable, versioned | Pick the one that matches your data volume, access patterns, and infrastructure constraints.
